Thinking the women had not heard his sermon, the Prophet went to them with Bilal and ordered them to give alms, and they gave earrings and rings into Bilal's garment.
The Prophet told a man whose mother died suddenly that she would be rewarded if he gave alms on her behalf.
Spending wealth rightly is worth envying; Allah grows charity from honest earnings; give now, for before the Hour a time will come when no one accepts charity.
A verse answered those mocking large and small gifts; companions worked as porters to give; half a date shields from Hell, as do daughters treated well; give while healthy.
The wife with the longest hand, first to follow the Prophet, loved charity; alms given unknowingly to a thief, adulteress and rich man may reform them; secret givers are shaded.
A wife giving food from home is rewarded, as are her husband and storekeeper; the best charity is from surplus, dependents first; the giver's hand is better than the beggar's.
The Prophet hurried to give away charity gold before night, had women give jewellery at Eid, urged interceding for those who ask, and told Asma not to withhold money.
Charity and good deeds done before Islam keep their reward; a wife giving food from her husband's house, and an honest storekeeper paying as told, are rewarded alongside the husband.
Angels pray daily for spenders and against misers, whose iron cloak never widens; every Muslim owes charity, by work, help or good deeds; passed-on charity reaches its place.
Umar was told not to buy back a horse he gave in charity; the Prophet's family eat no charity, but charity given to Barira became their gift.
A wife giving household food in charity without waste is rewarded, as are her husband and storekeeper; giving from his earnings without permission earns her half his reward.
When told to give in charity, the companions worked as porters in the market to earn a Mudd, though some later owned a hundred thousand.
Gathering a bundle of firewood and selling it is better than asking people, who may give or refuse.
The Prophet would have eaten a date fallen on the road, or on his bed, but for fear it was from Sadaqa.
Asma, whose only property came from Az-Zubair, was told to give in charity and not withhold or give reluctantly, lest Allah withhold from her.
Lending a milch animal is a fine charity, best of forty deeds; land is better given free than rented, and the Ansar's gifted palms were returned after Khaibar.
Charity is due for every joint of the body, and each day establishing justice among people earns the reward of charity.
The best charity is given while healthy, greedy and fearing poverty, not delayed to the deathbed, when the property already belongs to the heirs.
Sa'd gives a garden and must fulfil a vow for his dead mother; Ka'b keeps some property, Abu Talha's garden goes to relatives, and heirs give at the division.
Abu Talha gives his beloved garden Bairuha for Allah's sake and, on the Prophet's advice, divides it among relatives; a man gives a garden in charity for his dead mother.
Umar asks whether he may buy back the horse he gave in charity for fighting, and is told not to, for one should not take back charity.
The miser and the charitable are like two men in tight iron cloaks: giving spreads the giver's cloak over him, while the miser's rings tighten and will not widen.
Umar gave a horse for Allah's Cause and later saw it being sold; the Prophet told him not to buy it, as that would take back his charity.
Each joint owes daily charity: judging justly, helping a rider mount or load up, a good word, steps to prayer and removing harm from the road all count.
Umar wanted to buy back cheaply a horse he gave for Allah's Cause; the Prophet forbade it, likening one who takes back his gift to a dog swallowing its vomit.
The Prophet said the poor person is not the one a date or a morsel will satisfy, but the one who does not beg from people or show his poverty.
When alms were ordered, companions worked as porters to have something to give; hypocrites mocked small and large gifts alike, and a verse came about those who criticise voluntary givers.
The Prophet likened the charitable man and the miser to two men in iron cloaks, one widening as he gives and one tightening, showing it at his own shirt's opening.
If a Muslim plants something and a person or an animal eats of it, he is rewarded as if he had given it in charity.
Every Muslim owes charity, by working, helping the distressed, enjoining good or refraining from evil, and the Fire is warded off even with half a date or a kind word.
Had the Prophet gold like Mount Uhud, he would love to give it all away within three days, if anyone accepted it, keeping only enough to pay debts.
Allah takes charity of a date's value from honest earnings in His Right Hand and grows it like a foal into a mountain, for only good ascends to Him.
